Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve intent and certainty. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "
our neighborhood weather station sits on the roof of the Cedar Street community hall, above the garden entrance and away from the kitchen vents. It began operating in April 2019, when the neighborhood association put the station there to give residents local readings, rather than relying only on reports from the airport. The roof is 18 meters above the street, and the station is about 600 meters from the river path. These distances are measured from the front door of the hall and from the marked river-path entrance, which is perhaps not the only way to measure them, but it is how the association records the locations.

The equipment includes a temperature and humidity sensor inside a white, ventilated shield, a wind sensor on a short mast, and a tipping-bucket rain gauge. A small solar panel charges the battery, with a backup battery kept in a locked cabinet downstairs. The station sends readings to a tablet in the hall office every five minutes. The tablet stores a local copy for 30 days, while the association's public page displays hourly figures. The temperature sensor is usually a little warmer in direct afternoon sun than the station's shaded reference thermometer, so volunteers compare them before they post a note about an unusual reading. They do not change the sensor values during that comparison.

Mina Patel checks the station on Tuesday and Friday mornings, and two other volunteers cover the remaining days. Their routine is not especially complicated, though several small things can be missed when it is rushed. They look for loose cables, leaves around the rain-gauge funnel, water inside the sensor shield, and a battery icon on the tablet. They also write down the outdoor temperature from a handheld thermometer kept in the office. The handheld thermometer is not treated as a replacement for the station sensor; it is there to give the volunteers another reading to compare. Mina says, “If the screen is blank, I check the plug before I blame the weather.”

The station has a basic record book in a blue binder, and a digital maintenance sheet on the association laptop. The binder includes the date, the volunteer's initials, and a short note about what they saw. The digital sheet has those details, plus a field for the time of any reset. The two records are updated after each visit, although they are occasionally not perfectly matching because someone makes the paper entry first and forgets to copy one detail later. At the monthly meeting, Mina usually checks both records against the tablet history. If she cannot explain a difference, she marks it for follow-up instead of deciding which record is right. This way is somewhat slower, but it avoids hiding a discrepancy just to make the two records look tidy.

1. The rain gauge needs a different check in cold weather. A volunteer lifts the funnel cover and checks whether water can move through the narrow opening. If the funnel is frozen at the 7 a.m. visit, the volunteer records the gauge reading as an estimate, writes “frozen funnel” in both records, and does not pour warm water into the gauge. This condition matters because the station's hourly rainfall page uses the recorded value; a number entered as an estimate is marked differently from a normal gauge reading. When the funnel is clear, the volunteer can tip a measured amount of water through it and compare the tablet's total with the amount used. The measured-water check is done about once a month, but perhaps more often after a cleaning.

2. Wind readings have their own limits. The mast is fixed to a metal bracket near the roof's east edge, where the wind sensor has a clear path above the roofline. The hall's brick chimney is about four meters to the west, and the volunteers note that direction when they review unusual readings. They do not move the sensor to improve a single reading, since a different position would make the older and newer records harder to compare. The public page reports average wind speed and the highest gust recorded in each hour. It does not show a separate wind-direction chart, though the direction is saved in the tablet history. A loud clicking sound from the mast was reported once in October, but the volunteers found a loose cable tie, not a damaged sensor.

3. The association keeps the station available to the public without publishing details about individual volunteers. The page names the station and gives its location as Cedar Street, but it does not list home addresses or phone numbers. A small notice at the garden entrance explains that the equipment is for weather readings and should not be touched. The hall manager keeps a spare key for the roof hatch, while the volunteers use the office key during their checks. When a school group visits, they look at the tablet indoors rather than going up to the roof. Mina says, “The readings are more useful when people know what they can and cannot tell us.” The association has not arranged school visits on a fixed schedule; requests are considered when the hall is available.

During the winter, the station receives fewer visits from passersby, but the volunteer rota continues as usual. The association has set aside money for one replacement humidity sensor, though it has not ordered one because the current sensor is still reporting. The next planned task is to clean the solar panel and check the cabinet battery before the spring rainier period. If the tablet stops receiving readings for more than one day, Mina will contact the volunteer who manages the public page and they will check the connection together. The station is small, and its records are not a substitute for official forecasts, but the neighborhood uses them to compare conditions around Cedar Street with the airport report and to keep a local history of rain, temperature, and wind.", "output": "Our neighborhood weather station sits on the roof of the Cedar Street community hall, above the garden entrance and away from the kitchen vents.
